questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the parts of the ear in the order they are vibrated by sound waves?
options: Eardrum, tiny bones, and cochlea
Cochlea, tiny bones, and eardrum
Eardrum, auditory nerve, and brain
Cochlea, auditory nerve, and tiny bones

questions.question: What is the role of the specialized cells in the cochlea?
options: They block high-frequency sounds from entering the brain.
They vibrate to produce new sound waves inside the ear.
They sense vibrations and cause electrical signals to be sent along a nerve.
They directly create the physical sensation of hearing.

questions.question: What is the normal frequency range of hearing for human ears, and at which frequencies are they most sensitive?
options: 20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 2–5 kHz waves.
2 Hz to 200 Hz, being most sensitive to 20–50 Hz waves.
200 Hz to 200 kHz, being most sensitive to 2–5 kHz waves.
20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 10–15 kHz waves.

questions.question: As a sound wave travels through a medium, what is the motion of each bit of air?
options: It travels continuously forward alongside the wave energy.
It vibrates parallel to the direction of wave travel, without travelling forwards.
It moves in circles, gradually moving forward.
It oscillates up and down at 90 degrees to the direction of travel.

questions.question: What makes sound waves longitudinal waves?
options: The direction of vibration is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
The direction of vibration is parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
They can only travel through extremely long distances in air.
They do not require any particles or medium to transfer energy.

questions.question: Why does sound travel faster in solids and liquids than in gases?
options: The particles are further apart, giving the sound wave more room to move.
The particles are very close together, so vibrations are easily passed on.
Solids and liquids are always at a much higher temperature than gases.
The particles in solids and liquids vibrate at a much lower frequency naturally.

questions.question: What explains why sound waves travel faster in solids than in liquids?
options: The strong forces between particles in solids mean vibrations travel even faster.
The particles in solids are much lighter than those in liquids.
Solids have large gaps between their particles.
Liquids absorb all vibrations and prevent them from spreading.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the speed of sound?
options: It is about 340 m/s in air, slower in liquids, and slowest in solids.
It is about 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids, and faster still in solids.
It is about 1500 m/s in air, and cannot travel through solids.
It is constant at 340 m/s regardless of whether it is in a solid, liquid, or gas.

questions.question: What is the name of the sound heard when sound waves reflect from hard surfaces and travel back to the listener?
options: An echo
A refraction
An ultrasound
A superposition

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the speed of sound, why is it better to measure longer distances and times?
options: It ensures that any errors are a smaller proportion of the measurements.
It changes the speed of sound so that it is easier to calculate.
It prevents sound waves from reflecting off nearby objects.
It allows sound waves to travel faster than their normal speed.

questions.question: What are sound waves with a frequency above 20,000 Hz called, and can humans hear them?
options: Infrasound, and they are easily heard by humans.
Ultrasound, and they usually cannot be heard by humans.
Infrasound, and they usually cannot be heard by humans.
Ultrasound, and they are extremely loud to human ears.

questions.question: How is ultrasound used to produce images of structures inside the body?
options: It reflects from the boundaries between different tissues.
It passes completely through all tissues without any change.
It is absorbed by bones and heats them up to make them glow.
It changes the frequency of the body's cells to make them visible.

questions.question: Why are water waves classified as transverse waves?
options: The direction of oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
The direction of oscillation is 90 degrees to the direction of energy transfer.
The water particles travel all the way forward with the wave.
They do not involve any oscillation of water particles.

questions.question: What is the definition of the amplitude of a water wave?
options: The greatest distance water moves above and below the rest position.
The distance between two consecutive wave crests.
The number of waves that pass a certain point in one second.
The total speed at which the wave moves forward.

questions.question: What is the term for when waves pass through each other and either 'add up' or 'cancel out'?
options: Wave refraction
Wave superposition
Wave reflection
Wave absorption
